articles.headline: Your Stress Is Slowly Reshaping Your Heart. New Data Shows Why.
articles.body: A massive study of nearly half a million UK adults found that chronic stress linked to everyday life—money worries, mental health struggles, your job—triggers persistent inflammation that quietly damages your heart's structure years before you feel anything wrong. People with the highest inflammation levels faced a 43% greater risk of heart attack and stroke. The kicker: these changes happen silently, appearing on imaging scans long before symptoms show up. Researchers used cardiac MRI and AI to track how stress-induced inflammation actually changes your heart's shape, thickening walls and shrinking chambers.
articles.takeaway: Check your inflammation markers before symptoms appear. Stress management isn't luxury—it's cardiology.
articles.source: European Journal of Preventive Cardiology / Imperial College London

articles.headline: More REM Sleep Cuts Your Disease Risk by Half. 95,000 People Tracked.
articles.body: Forget just sleeping longer. A landmark study of 95,000 adults wearing wrist trackers for nine years found that people spending more time in REM sleep—the stage where you dream—had significantly lower risks of 83 different diseases, including dementia, heart failure, and Parkinson's. The effect was dramatic: more REM sleep meant lower dementia risk (54% reduction), lower heart failure risk, and protection against multiple serious conditions. Deep sleep protected against seven conditions like type 2 diabetes. The sweet spot: 6-8 hours total, uninterrupted. People sleeping less than five hours faced much higher disease risk across dozens of conditions.
articles.takeaway: Your dream sleep matters more than you think. Protect 6-8 unbroken hours like it's your insurance policy.

articles.topic: Aerobic exercise brain age reversal MRI
articles.headline: One Year of Exercise Just Made Your Brain a Year Younger. Literally.
articles.body: Adults who followed basic aerobic exercise guidelines—150 minutes per week of moderate activity—had brains that looked almost a full year younger on MRI scans after 12 months compared to people who didn't exercise. Using AI trained on thousands of brain scans, researchers measured 'brain age'—how old your brain appears versus your actual age. The exercisers' brains improved by about 0.6 years. The control group's brains aged 0.35 years. That one-year gap matters: prior research links every extra year of brain aging to roughly 3% higher dementia risk later. The study covered middle-aged adults doing regular cardio—nothing extreme.
articles.takeaway: Your 150-minute weekly workout isn't just making your heart stronger. It's literally reversing your brain's aging clock.
articles.source: Journal of Sport and Health Science

articles.headline: This Plant Compound Sharpens Your Focus Better Than Caffeine Alone.
articles.body: Guarana—an Amazonian plant packed with caffeine and other compounds—improved speed and accuracy on demanding cognitive tasks better than caffeine alone, according to multiple studies. When combined with vitamins and minerals, guarana reduced mental fatigue during sustained mental effort and improved both reaction time and accuracy on rapid visual information processing tests. Interestingly, the effect wasn't just from the caffeine: low doses of guarana (75 mg containing only 9 mg caffeine) still improved performance, suggesting the plant's other compounds matter. Students taking guarana showed strong improvements in energy, memory, and attention—and more people noticed guarana's effects than green tea.
articles.takeaway: If you're choosing between energy drinks, guarana hits different. The plant compounds work where caffeine alone taps out.

workout.title: Hill Repeat Foundation: Gradual Intensity Climbing
workout.tip: Lean slightly into the hill and shorten your stride—don't overstride uphill. Use your arms to drive forward and up. Downhill should be a true recovery jog, not a sprint, so your legs don't accumulate extra fatigue.
workout.warmup: 5 min: easy jog on flat ground, then 4 x 15 sec gradual accelerations (building effort) with 45 sec walk recovery between each

exercises.name: Hill Repeat Block
exercises.reps: 60–90 sec uphill at hard effort / jog down easy recovery
exercises.notes: Find a hill with a 4–6% grade (noticeable but not steep). Run up at a pace where you're breathing hard but can still say a word or two. Jog down slowly to recover. Each repeat should feel manageable; you should finish feeling like you could do one more.

workout.cooldown: 4 min easy jog on flat, then 1 min walk. Calf stretch against wall 20 sec each leg, quad stretch 20 sec each leg, glute figure-four stretch 20 sec each side.
workout.description: A controlled hill-repeat session designed for beginners to build leg strength and running power without excessive impact. By running uphill at moderate intensity with downhill recovery, you safely introduce lactate work while improving 5K and 10K race capability.

meal.title: Seared Tuna and Edamame Rice Bowl with Sesame Ginger Glaze
meal.description: Do not overcook the tuna. Pull it the moment the outside turns opaque. Overcooking dries it out and kills the texture. Sixty seconds per side on screaming-hot heat is all you need.
meal.instructions:
Ingredients:
2 ahi tuna steaks (approx. 5 oz each)
1 cup cooked brown rice
1 cup shelled edamame (thawed from frozen)
1 tbsp low-sodium soy sauce
1 tsp sesame oil
1 tsp fresh grated ginger
1 tsp honey
1 clove garlic, minced
1 tbsp olive oil (for searing)
1 tsp sesame seeds
2 scallions, sliced
Lime wedge for serving

Instructions:
1. Mix soy sauce, sesame oil, ginger, honey, and garlic in a small bowl. Set aside. 2. Pat tuna steaks dry, season lightly with salt and pepper. Heat olive oil in a skillet over high heat and sear tuna for 60-90 seconds per side, leaving the center pink. Remove and slice. 3. In the same pan over medium heat, warm edamame for 2 minutes then toss with half the glaze. 4. Build the bowl: brown rice on the bottom, edamame and sliced tuna on top. Drizzle with remaining glaze and finish with sesame seeds and scallions.
